reason: The cited evidence (E1, E2) supports dislocation-mediated deformation and toughening at nanoscale FCC/BCC phase boundaries in MPEAs, but it addresses room-temperature tensile properties, not high-temperature creep resistance. No evidence is provided for sustained loading at ~1000 °C, cyclic conditions, or creep rate reduction, leaving key premises about creep behavior and high-temperature efficacy unsupported.
premises: Nanoscale FCC/BCC phase boundaries can be engineered in high-entropy alloys via rapid solidification or additive manufacturing.
Such phase boundaries enable continuous dislocation bridging and transfer between FCC and BCC phases.
Dislocation bridging uniformly distributes plastic strain and delays localized deformation.
This mechanism enhances creep resistance (lower steady-state creep rate) under sustained high-temperature loading.
The approach is effective at ~1000 °C under cyclic loading conditions.
